title: Mediator pattern
idea: The Mediator pattern routes all coordination between related objects through one mediator, so each colleague knows the mediator instead of every other colleague.

analogy.text: Planes near an airport talk to the control tower, never to each other. The tower decides who lands next.
analogy.breaks: A tower improvises; a code mediator follows fixed rules.

points: Colleagues report changes to the mediator; the mediator decides who reacts and how.
Each colleague needs one link to the hub, not one to every sibling.
UI dialogs and MVC controllers often mediate between widgets and the model.
Skip it for two collaborators; one mediator for everything becomes a god class.

hero.title: Widgets report only to the form

steps.caption: Each input field holds one reference: the mediator. No field can reach a sibling.
Quantity is set to 0. The field stores it and calls `changed(this)`, nothing more.
The mediator applies the rules in one place: recompute the total, switch ordering off.
A coupon is entered. The coupon field also reports only to the mediator.
The same rules run again. The total cannot go negative and ordering stays off.
Quantity becomes 2. Again one report, one place that decides.
Now there is something to buy, so the mediator turns the order button on.

code.title: The problem: wired widgets
code.caption: Each widget calls the others directly, so one rule is copied into two places.

walk.text: Every field is built with references to its siblings; the two fields even point at each other.
The quantity field owns the total and button rules itself.
The coupon field copies those rules, and the copy forgot the `qty > 0` check.
After quantity 0 and a coupon, the total goes negative and ordering is enabled.

code.title: The fix: one mediator
code.caption: Widgets report changes; one mediator holds every rule that spans widgets.

walk.text: The mediator interface has one method: a colleague says it changed.
The base widget knows only `FormMediator`. It has no way to reach a sibling.
A field validates its own input, stores it and reports. It holds no form rules.
The concrete mediator owns every widget and attaches itself to the two input fields.
Every cross-widget rule lives here once: discount, clamped total, when ordering is allowed.
The same steps as before now keep the total sane and the button honest.

pitfalls: Letting a widget call a sibling "just once" rebuilds the tangle; route everything through the mediator.
Putting a whole screen's business logic in one mediator creates a god class; split by feature.
A mediator that updates a colleague which reports back can loop forever; guard re-entrant changes.

quiz.q: Five services each call the other four to coordinate a checkout. Which change applies the Mediator pattern?
options: Add a coordinator that all five report to
Put an interface on each service
Merge the five services into one class
quiz.why: A mediator replaces many-to-many calls with one hub. Interfaces and singletons keep every link; merging throws away the separate responsibilities.

takeaway: Colleagues talk to the mediator, never to each other.

starters: How is the Mediator pattern different from the Observer pattern?
